blocks.text: Dear Ms. Lewis:

This letter confirms our engagement to prepare the bridge deck rehabilitation design for {{fact:f:E-2007-001.client}}. It sets out the scope of the work, the fee, and the terms under which we will proceed. Signed and returned, one copy of it stands as our agreement. I have kept it plain, so that it records what we discussed and asks nothing you did not expect from that conversation.
The Work

We will prepare a rehabilitation design for the bridge deck. The scope covers the assessment of the existing deck condition, from the record drawings you provide and from our own field observation; the design of the concrete repairs and the wearing surface; the deck drainage and the treatment of the joints; and the traffic and staging notes the work will require. The set will be prepared to the standard the reviewing authority expects at submittal, and the cover sheet will be issued under seal.

We will coordinate the Peck-Jennings deck rehabilitation design as a single set, so that the repair details, the drainage, and the staging agree with one another before the drawings are sealed. On a rehabilitation, the observed condition governs the design, and so the repair limits and the quantities will follow from our examination of the deck rather than from the record drawings alone. Where our design meets work that is properly the contractor's or another party's, our sheets will note the interface and stop there. The scope does not extend to construction-phase inspection or to material testing. We would take up either of those separately if you wished, on terms we would set at that time.

We will assemble the completed sheets as a package suitable for the reviewing authority, and we will respond to the comments that come back on it as part of this design. Should a review require substantial rework beyond the ordinary, I will raise it with you before that work proceeds. The aim throughout is a set a contractor can build the rehabilitation from and a reviewer can approve without guesswork.
Our Approach

I walk a structure before I draw it, and I run the quantities myself rather than accept a figure I have not checked. The design will proceed from your record drawings and from our own observation of the deck as it stands, and I will hold the set to what the field conditions will actually support. We will keep you informed as the design develops, in short progress reports and in meetings when a decision is yours to make, and we will not let a question that is yours to decide sit unasked. Nothing leaves this office until it has been reviewed on my desk and I am satisfied it is correct. I, Mark Todd, will direct the work and seal each sheet before it is issued.
Assigned Staff

The design will be carried by our engineering staff. Pamela Warren, our Project Engineer, will handle the deck drainage and the coordination with the reviewing authority, and she will cite the governing standard on each detail before it is drawn. Jason Jordan will prepare the roadway, approach, and staging sheets and keep the standard details current across the set. Kimberly Branch will draft the repair details and run the quantity takeoffs that stand behind the fee. I will review and seal the completed set myself.
Fee and Commencement

Our fee for the design is {{fact:f:E-2007-001.fee}}, a fixed amount for the scope described above. We will begin the work on {{fact:f:E-2007-001.start}}. The design is a compact one, and we expect it to run about four months from commencement, subject to the timeliness of the record information and of the reviews on your side. If the scope changes in a way that bears on the fee, I will raise it with you, and we will settle it before any additional work proceeds.
Fees and Payment

We will invoice against the fee monthly as the work proceeds, and our invoices are due within thirty days of receipt. The fee covers our staff and their time. It does not cover out-of-pocket costs such as reproduction, delivery, and agency or permit fees; those we bill at cost. Where such a cost is of any consequence, we will agree it with you before it is incurred, and a small and routine one we will simply carry on the next invoice.
Term and Termination

Either of us may end this engagement on fourteen days written notice. If {{fact:f:E-2007-001.client}} ends it, you will owe us for the work properly performed to that date and for costs already committed on your behalf, and nothing further. On termination we will deliver the work in progress in the form it then stands, and the drawings remain your property to the extent you have paid for them.
Confidentiality

We will treat the information you provide in the course of this work as confidential and use it only for this design. That obligation binds our whole staff and continues after the engagement ends. Drawings we seal and issue become part of the project record in the ordinary course, and nothing in this paragraph restricts that.
Limitation of Liability

We will perform the design with the care and skill ordinarily exercised by civil engineers practicing in this area at this time, and we stand behind our work to that standard. We do not warrant the performance of contractors or others we do not control, nor the results of construction carried out from our drawings without our involvement. Our liability to you under this engagement is limited to the amount of our fee, except where the law does not permit such a limit.
Governing Law

This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which our firm practices, and any dispute under it will be heard in the courts of that state. Should any single provision be found unenforceable, the remainder of this letter stands.
If these terms reflect our understanding, please sign both copies below, keep one for your files, and return the other to this office. On receipt I will schedule the field visit and begin the work.
Very truly yours,

The bridge deck rehabilitation design for {{fact:f:E-2007-001.client}} is under way, with our start set for {{fact:f:E-2007-001.start}}. This memo sets the assignments and the opening tasks, so that the project folder is in order from the beginning and no one is left waiting on a hand-off that was never made. The aim of the first weeks is narrow and practical: to open the lettered project folder, bring in the record drawings and the field notes, and set up the sheet index and the standard details, so that when the design proper begins the file is already clean.

The work itself is straightforward in kind, if not in effort. We are rehabilitating an existing deck, which means the record information and the observed condition govern the design more than they would on new work, and a repair detail is only as good as the condition it is drawn to answer. The value in these opening weeks lies in getting the file and the field information right, so that the design that follows rests on something firm rather than on assumption.
Assignments

items: Jason Jordan: the roadway, approach, and staging sheets, the border sheets, and the standard details, each confirmed current before we build on it.
Pamela Warren, Project Engineer: the deck drainage and the coordination with the reviewing authority, and the governing standards the repair details must answer to.
Kimberly Branch: the deck repair details and the quantity takeoffs, filed and labeled so a number can be found again when the set is revisited.
Carol Lewis, Director of Operations, is our point of contact at the client; approvals and questions on their side route through her.

blocks.text: A word on the file itself. Every sheet is matched to the memorandum or the standard that governs it, and revisions are clouded and logged as they are made, so that the current sheet can be pulled in a hurry when the client calls. Please keep to that discipline from the first print, because a set that is kept orderly as it is drawn stays orderly through to issue.

Coordination with the client runs through Carol Lewis. When we need a decision or a document from their side, one of us asks her rather than several of us asking around, so that the requests stay in order and nothing is asked twice. The same holds for anything that leaves the office: a transmittal notes what was issued and when, so that the folder keeps a record of every set sent out, and the review order is not to be shortcut, since no sheet goes out until it has been checked and the cover sheet sealed.
First tasks

items: Open the lettered project folder for the Peck-Jennings deck rehabilitation and set up the sheet index and the title blocks.
Bring in the record drawings and confirm they are the current ones before any repair is drawn over them.
Walk the deck with an engineer and note the observed conditions against the record, so the repair quantities start from what is actually there.
Set up the standard details and the border sheets so the set reads the firm's way from the first sheet.

blocks.text: The first thing we need is the record set. I will confirm with Carol Lewis's office that we hold the current record drawings before we build the base, and until that base is right nothing drawn over it can be trusted. Once it is in hand, we begin.

Minutes of the progress meeting on the {{fact:f:E-2007-001.client}} bridge deck rehabilitation design, held at the firm's office and recorded by Kimberly Branch. The meeting reviewed the state of the field assessment, the design in progress, and the coordination between the drainage and the repair details, and it settled the items to be carried before the next session.
Attendees

items: Pamela Warren, Project Engineer, Brackenridge Civil Group
Jason Jordan, Design Technician, Brackenridge Civil Group
Kimberly Branch, Design Technician, Brackenridge Civil Group
Carol Lewis, Director of Operations, Peck-Jennings

blocks.text: Discussion

Pamela Warren opened with the state of the field assessment. The deck has been walked and the visible spalling and delamination mapped, and the record drawings have been reconciled against the observed conditions. She noted that the deck drainage will govern several of the repair details, and that the governing standard will be cited on each sheet before the detail is drawn, so that the approach can survive the reviewing authority's read.

Jason Jordan reported on the roadway, approach, and staging sheets. The base sheets are set up and the standard details have been brought current, and the staging concept is being drawn to keep at least one lane open through the work. He flagged one inconsistency between the record deck section and the field measurements, which he will carry to the engineer of record before the repair limits are fixed.

Kimberly Branch reported that the repair details are in progress and that a preliminary quantity takeoff has been started from the mapped repair areas, to be firmed up as the details are completed. Carol Lewis asked that the client be kept informed of any finding that would bear on the cost or the schedule, and it was agreed that material questions would be raised with her office as they arise rather than held for the next meeting.

The group also discussed how the record drawings and the field notes are held in the project folder, so that the sheet in hand is always the current one and a repair detail can be traced back to the condition it answers. It was noted that the drainage design and the repair details must be coordinated as one, since the placement of a drain or a joint bears directly on the extent of the repair around it, and that this coordination should be checked before either is carried much further.

On schedule, the group agreed that the design remains in its early stage, with the assessment substantially in hand and the detailing under way, and that the coordination between the drainage and the repair details is the item most likely to govern the pace of the coming weeks. No item was identified as being at risk of delaying the set, though the reconciliation of the record section with the field measurements was noted as the first thing that must be settled.
Action items

rows: Reconcile the record deck section with the field measurements and confirm the repair limits
Before the repair details are advanced
Complete the deck drainage layout and cite the governing standard on each detail
Firm up the repair quantity takeoff as the details are completed
With the next set of details
Relay any cost or schedule finding to the client's office

blocks.text: The next progress meeting will be set once the repair details are advanced. These minutes will be circulated to the attendees, and any correction should be returned to Kimberly Branch.
Summary of Progress

The bridge deck rehabilitation design for {{fact:f:E-2007-001.client}} is at roughly its midpoint and is proceeding on plan. The field assessment of the deck is complete, the repair details and the deck drainage are well advanced, and the set is moving toward the coordinated stage at which it can be assembled for the reviewing authority. The work remains within the fixed design fee of {{fact:f:E-2007-001.fee}}, and nothing observed to date has called either the scope or the budget into question. It continues to be carried by the same staff who began it, and the coordination that governs a rehabilitation set, between the observed condition, the repair details, and the drainage, has been held close from the start.
Accomplishments This Period

Since the last report, Pamela Warren has completed the deck drainage layout and has begun the coordination with the reviewing authority, citing the governing standard on each detail so that the approach is settled before the set is carried further. The repair details, drawn by Kimberly Branch from the mapped areas of spalling and delamination, are now substantially complete, and the quantity takeoff that stands behind the fee has been firmed up against them so that the numbers rest on the conditions actually observed rather than on a general allowance.

The assessment work that underlies all of this is now closed out. The deck was walked in full, and the joints and the existing wearing surface were examined along with the areas of distress, so that the findings could be carried onto the plans and the repair details drawn to answer the deck that was observed. That closure is what allows the detailing and the takeoff to proceed with confidence at this stage, and it is the reason the scope has held steady since the work began.

On the roadway and staging side, the approach and staging sheets have been developed to keep at least one lane open through construction, and the standard details have been brought current across the set. The inconsistency noted earlier between the record deck section and the field measurements has since been reconciled, and the repair limits have been fixed accordingly, so that the quantities now rest on the Peck-Jennings deck as it actually stands rather than on the record drawings alone.
Work of the Coming Period

The work of the coming weeks is coordination and completion rather than new design. Pamela Warren will carry the drainage and the repair details through the reviewing authority's comments as they return, and Kimberly Branch will hold the quantities current against any change those comments require, so that the takeoff and the drawings do not drift apart. The staging sheets will be coordinated a final time against the repair sequence, so that the traffic scheme and the work it protects remain consistent through construction.

The internal check will then be run before anything is sealed, in keeping with the firm's practice that no set leaves the office until it has been reviewed and the cover sheet sealed. The set will be assembled, checked, and prepared for sealing, at which point it will be issued under the firm's cover sheet as a package a contractor can build the rehabilitation from and a reviewer can approve without guesswork.
Risks and Items to Watch

Two items warrant attention. The first is the reviewing authority's turnaround, which is outside the firm's control and could move the completion of the set if comments are slow to return; we have front-loaded the coordination with the authority in order to limit that exposure as far as we are able. The second is the possibility that a repair area proves more extensive on closer examination than the visible condition suggested, which would bear on the quantities rather than on the design approach, and which we would bring to your office promptly should it develop, along with its effect, if any, on the design fee of {{fact:f:E-2007-001.fee}}.

Neither item is regarded as a present threat to the work, and both are being watched in the ordinary course rather than managed as a problem. The repair quantities are the figure most sensitive to what the review and the closer detailing turn up, and so they are the number we will keep under the closest eye as the set is finished, so that any movement in them is seen while there is still time to account for it.

Taken together, the engagement is where it should be at its midpoint. The assessment is behind us, the detailing is nearly done, and the set is moving toward the review and the seal within the terms agreed at the outset, with the same staff carrying it through that began it. We will continue to track the work against the plan as the details close out, and we will bring anything of consequence to your office as soon as it appears rather than hold it for the next report.

The next step is to complete the coordinated set and prepare it for review, and we will report again as it goes out. Should you wish to discuss any part of the work before then, Jason Jordan can be reached at the firm's office.
